items.title: Ask HN: Windows Signing for FOSS Projects
items.summary: Hey, all. I'm wondering how people handle signing packages for Windows when your project is open-source and there is no budget for an expensive code-signing certificate. I thought I had found a solution with SignPath's (https://signpath.org/) free certs for open source, but I ran into two snags with them. - I can't use custom runners in my github workflow. I was using a larger runner (still github hosted, I just picked a larger size) to run my tests faster, and SignPath failed the job because it didn't recognize the runner name. So I would have to go back to a standard runner with a name they recognize, which runs my tests about 3x slower. - I have to approve each package signing, which means that a release process that was fully automated now has a step I have to manually approve. I raised both of these issues with SignPath over a week ago, and I have yet to get a response, or to even have my signing certificate issued. So I'm about to give up on them. Windows is only about 10% of my user base, so right now I'm leaning towards just continuing to not sign my Windows releases. But before I throw in the towel, I wanted to ask if anyone here knows of a better way to handle this. Oh, and shameless plug for my project, a kubernetes management app: https://github.com/luxury-yacht/app/

items.title: Took apart Claude Code, then turned it into a free course on harness engineering
items.summary: The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch. Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness. Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood. And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales. On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. Ramp scaling its operations with a custom harness is a perfect example. So I turned what I learned into an in-depth course on harness engineering by building Claude Code from scratch. It's free and open source: 8 articles, 6 videos, and one codebase. It's perfect for people who learn by building. Everything in Python. For full transparency, Modal, Opik, and Kitaru sponsor the course, which lets me keep it 100% free as an independent AI engineer. Here are the 8 steps that I think are core to building and maintaining any harness: 1. Design the harness 2. Build the bare-bones agent loop 3. Sandbox it, locally and remotely 4. Apply 4 essential context engineering techniques 5. Add subagents as a context engineering technique 6. Deploy it headless to the cloud: CLI, webhooks, cron 7. Build benchmarks to measure it 8. Replay failed runs to debug agents Everything is on GitHub: https://github.com/decodingai-magazine/building-a-coding-agent-from-scratch-course Curious what others here think. Which of these steps has been the hardest to get right in your own agents?
